title: Hope in Resurrection
english: From Cyril: At the impious deeds of the Jews, those they committed against Christ, the very nature of the elements was distressed, and creation, so to speak, broke into lament at the sight of its own Master outraged. The divine temple, as though it were nearly as grieved as the mourners, was torn right through; for it is written that “the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). The sun bound up its own blaze, drew in its rays, and would no longer deign to shine on those on the earth, for it brought darkness from the sixth hour to the ninth (Matthew 27:45). The rocks, too, were split. And perhaps something unusual was also happening around the disk of the moon, so that it too seemed to have been changed into blood.

The holy evangelists pass over this in silence, but prophecy gives trustworthy proof of it. At the Creator’s command the signs did not appear in the sun alone; the whole creation, as it were, passed into a state without beauty and strange to it. This would be made plain by the voice of Isaiah, who says: “And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth” (Isaiah 50:3). When he says “heaven,” he surely means everything in heaven. He says he will wrap it in dark sackcloth, as it were, like one mourning and stricken with grief, and crying out by this very garb.

These, then, I would call the signs or wonders in heaven. But those on earth, “blood and fire and vapor of smoke” (Acts 2:19), would point, I think, to the disasters of the Jews, which the most grievous war, waged by the hand of the Romans, heaped upon them. Their whole land was spattered with blood; the famous temple itself was about to be burned along with the cities, and houses, shaken to the ground, to send up smoke.

That such things will befall the Jews even before the great and manifest day, on which the divine judgment seat will be set before all, with Christ giving to each according to his works, he made plain when he said: “Before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Acts 2:20).
“Moreover my flesh also will dwell in hope” (Acts 2:26).

From Cyril: For he came back to life on the third day, since it was not possible for him, being life by nature, to be held by the bonds of death (Acts 2:24). And again: For it is not right to say that the flesh united to the Word could ever be held by corruption, or that the divine soul became a captive of the very gates of Hades. He was not left in Hades (Acts 2:31), as the inspired Peter also said.
“For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your Holy One see corruption” (Acts 2:27).
From Cyril: For he came back to life after plundering Hades and saying to those in bonds, “Come out,” and to those in darkness, “Be uncovered” (Isaiah 49:9).
“You have made known to me the ways of life” (Acts 2:28).

From Cyril of Alexandria: He is teaching this: the one who became as we are, bearing the person of humanity, utters words that suit us rather than himself, insofar as he is understood to be God, as though calling down, first on himself and then on us, the…

added_allusions.reason: 'giving to each according to his works' echoes the judgment formula (also Matthew 16:27); not a marked quotation, so no reference is printed.

translator_notes: The Greek is fragmented at the end of p20 with 'upon us the', suggesting a cut mid-phrase; no completion attempted.
p6, p12, p18 are editorial attributions ('Κυρίλλου', 'Κυρίλλου Ἀλεξανδρείας') and treated as non-content; skipped per instructions.
p5 contains '74.761' which appears as a stray digit or folio marker; omitted as non-content.
The text switches between oratio obliqua and direct speech; preserved as given.
Some phrases like 'shmeared' or unclear compounds are rendered literally per lexicon; no conjectural emendation.

title: Divine Humility and Authority
english: …share in the heavenly goods. For what he says has been given to himself, he assigns to human nature, since in some way we have been made rich by the poverty of the man.
“Whom God raised from the dead, by him this man stands before you healthy” (Acts 4:10).

From Cyril: No one would doubt that the Father is said to have raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, the deed plainly being worked on his flesh. And he himself, being the life-giving and active power of the Father, was giving life to his own temple, as in the saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). So what was given life was not something foreign to him, nor the body of one of the men like us, but the very own body of the Word himself.
“Men, brothers and fathers, listen to me” (Acts 7:2).
From Cyril of Alexandria: He tells them to make themselves ready to be teachable, and, as if bending down their ear, to grasp closely the force of the divine words.
“Go out from your land and from your kindred,” and so on (Acts 7:3).

From Cyril: See, then: those who follow God wholly and in every way, and who have put the things of the flesh and worldly love of pleasure second to their hope in him, will surely be granted a rich share in the blessing from above.
“And Moses was trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was mighty in his words and deeds. When he was reaching the age of forty…” (Acts 7:22–23).
From Saint Cyril: That is why Christ also said, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). For theirs are the promises, theirs the fathers (Romans 9:4–5).

From the same: Or are we not to grant that the Word from God the Father, when he came to be in our condition, that is, a man, all but stepped out, and are we not to say that he came to be outside the glory that befits God, if it is true that “though he was rich, he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9), and let himself down into self-emptying?
“But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him away, saying, ‘Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’” (Acts 7:27–28).

From Cyril of Alexandria: The inspired Moses was accused of having killed the Egyptian, even though the Egyptian was the oppressor and the attacker. And when Christ was burying the evil demons, as it were, in the abyss, putting one who was unwilling out of his tyranny over us, and driving them out of those who had them, they said, when he ought to have been admired for this: “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons” (Matthew 12:24).
“I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob” (Acts 7:32).

From Cyril: Notice the weakness of the law. The God of all shows himself, but as he makes himself manifest, Moses turns away his face. This too would be a clear sign to us that the children of Israel could not gaze on the Son’s glory, the glory that befits God, even when he was showing himself and all but leading them to know him.
“And the Lord said to him, ‘Take off…

added_allusions.reason: 'made rich by the poverty of the man' in the first paragraph echoes the verse; not quoted, so no reference there (the verse is cited where it is quoted later in the section).
'let himself down into self-emptying' (καθῆκεν ἑαυτὸν εἰς κένωσιν) echoes ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν; paraphrase, no reference printed.
Moses turning away his face at the bush; Cyril paraphrases, no reference printed.

translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the edges.
The translation of 'ἐπεί πως' as 'somehow' is an attempt to convey the reason for human enrichment.
The phrase 'τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσει' is translated as 'human nature', indicating the recipient of the action.
The word 'ἐν τούτῳ οὖτος' is translated as 'he', referring back to the subject of the sentence, Jesus Christ.
The allusion to 2 Corinthians 8:9 is based on the phrase 'being rich, he became poor', which is a reference to Christ's humility.

title: Removal of Corruption
english: …the sandal from your feet’” (Acts 7:33).

From Cyril: The thing is a sign of deadness and corruption, since every sandal is the remains of an animal already dead and decayed. So Christ cannot be approached by those who live under the law and its worship that served as a tutor. One must first wash off the defilement and first scrub away the filth that comes from sin.
“And I will deport you beyond Babylon” (Acts 7:43).
From Cyril: Since you have filled up the wickedness of the Moabites, of Damascus your neighbor, for that very reason you will be carried off beyond Damascus, that is, to Babylon.
“And he asked to find a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Acts 7:46).
From Cyril: “For I will take no rest,” he says, “until I learn the place of the Lord and the dwelling (that is, the tabernacle) of the God of Jacob” (Psalm 132:5), and plainly that means Christ.
“But Solomon built him a house. Yet the Most High does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 7:47–48).

From Cyril: The most wise Solomon built that famous temple in Jerusalem, and the people of the Jews took great delight in it and supposed that the God of all dwelt in it, enclosed there. For they are always somehow slow to understand and ignorant of what is said about God. They even thought Jerusalem was God’s city and insisted that he dwelt in it alone, because of what is said by the voice of David: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 87:3). So God rebukes them for their petty notions and says, “What kind of house will you build for me, when I have heaven for a throne and earth for a footstool?” (Isaiah 66:1).
“And they stoned Stephen as he called out in prayer and said, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’” (Acts 7:59).
From Saint Cyril, on “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” (Luke 23:46): Again, a great and exceptional achievement for our souls…
“And he knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, ‘Lord, do not hold this sin against them.’ And when he had said this, he fell asleep” (Acts 7:60). “And Saul approved of his killing” (Acts 8:1).

From the same: For he says “Lord” as though defending himself, to show that even his earlier words had not come from anger, and wishing in this way to win them over. Letting go of anger and wrath at his own murder, and having his soul cleansed of that passion, made his words easy to accept.

From the same: And this blessed man does not pray in a casual way, but with attention, on his knees. See how godlike his death is: until that moment the Master allowed his soul to remain in him. At the very outset of the preaching, Stephen was overflowing beyond any river, silencing everyone; he stopped the shameless tongues of the Jews, and no one could stand against him (Acts 6:10); he threw the whole Jewish cause into confusion and set up a brilliant trophy and a conspicuous victory. This noble and wise man, full of grace, who was of such great help to the Church, had not spent long in the preaching when he was snatched away all at once, condemned as a blasphemer, and stoned.

added_allusions.reason: Cyril's note on Acts 7:43 reads 'beyond Damascus', the prophet's own wording; no reference printed in the note.

The translation tries to follow the original word order as closely as possible, while still producing natural literary prose.

The old English turned the catena heading 'Τοῦ ἁγίου Κυρίλλου εἰς τὸ Πάτερ, εἰς χεῖράς σου...' into narration ('As the holy Cyril says, I commit my spirit into your hands'), glued that cut-off excerpt to Acts 7:60, repeated one sentence four times ('remove the stain ... dirt ... filth'), and dropped the tags. Now the heading is a lead-in, the excerpt ends with '…' where the Greek breaks off, and the two 'Τοῦ αὐτοῦ' notes are each 'From the same:'. The Moabites and Damascus stand side by side with no conjunction, as in the print. The edition's variant '[Cod. διεγίνοντο]' (for διετείνοντο), column number 74.765 and page number 3 are not printed.
